Consult Summary:
- 19-year-old female with several days of dysuria, suprapubic crampy pain, malodorous urine and an episode of visible hematuria; clinician diagnosed likely acute uncomplicated cystitis and planned empirical oral antibiotics (patient advised fluids, avoidance of sex while symptomatic, and follow-up if no improvement).

History:
- Presenting complaint: Painful/stinging urination for a few days with lower abdominal (suprapubic), crampy discomfort; one episode of visible blood in urine earlier today; urine smells "a bit weird."
- Timeline: Symptoms started "a few days" ago; not improving with OTC bicarbonate taken a couple of days ago.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: No specific aggravating factors reported; OTC bicarbonate tried with no benefit; clinician advised increased fluids and cranberry juice as supportive measures.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Denies increased urinary frequency or urgency.
  - Denies vaginal discharge (patient asked and reported none).
  - Denies fever, chills, nausea, vomiting.
  - Denies flank or back pain.
  - Bowel habits: no diarrhea or change reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No fever reported.
  - No flank pain or systemic symptoms.
  - No noted vaginal discharge.

Past Medical History:
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
- No other chronic medical conditions documented.
- No relevant family history of kidney/bladder disease reported.

Medications:
- No regular prescription medications documented.
- Recent self-treatment: over-the-counter bicarbonate (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Antibiotics discussed: Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim recommended by clinician; clinician advised "one tablet twice a day for three days" but specific medication dose/route not documented.
- Allergies:
  - Clindamycin — swelling when taken (patient-reported).

Social History:
- Lives in a flat with friends near college.
- Occupation/education: Student studying biology.
- Sexual history: Sexually active with one boyfriend for a couple of months; uses condoms; reports never having had an STI screen.
- Tobacco: Denies smoking.
- Alcohol: Drinks socially on weekends.
- No other substance use documented.
- Advised to avoid sexual activity while symptomatic; continue barrier contraception if used.

Family History:
- No known family history of kidney, bladder, bowel disease reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: No formal vitals recorded; patient reported no fever.
- Physical exam findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- No investigations documented or performed in the consult (no urine dipstick/urinalysis, urine culture, STI NAAT, pregnancy test, or imaging recorded).
- Clinician recommended a pregnancy test to rule out pregnancy if concerned (patient denied being pregnant).

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (bladder infection) — aligns with clinician assessment and the DDx (high likelihood).

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Acute uncomplicated cystitis — supporting: dysuria, suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine, visible hematuria, sexually active young female; opposing: no frequency/urgency and no urinalysis documented.
- 2) Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — supporting: sexually active with no prior STI screen, dysuria possibly without discharge; opposing: malodorous urine, suprapubic pain and hematuria more typical of cystitis.
- 3) Urolithiasis (lower urinary tract stone) — supporting: hematuria and lower abdominal pain can occur with stone; opposing: lack of severe colicky flank/groin pain, and infection signs favor cystitis.
- No direct contradiction between transcript and DDx; DDx was used to organize alternative considerations.

Issue 1: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (dysuria, suprapubic pain)
- Assessment:
  - Most likely diagnosis per clinician and supported by symptoms.
- Plan:
  - Empiric oral antibiotic therapy offered: Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim — clinician stated "one tablet twice a day for three days." (Specific antibiotic selection and medication dose/route/frequency not documented.)
  - Advise increased oral fluids to help clear infection.
  - Supportive measure: cranberry juice suggested by clinician.
  - Sexual activity advice: avoid sex while symptomatic; continue barrier contraception if used.
  - Safety-netting: return/call if symptoms worsen, develop fever, flank/back pain, or not improved by end of the week.

Issue 2: Hematuria (single episode earlier today)
- Assessment:
  - Likely secondary to lower urinary tract inflammation/infection given presentation, but requires reassessment if persistent.
- Plan:
  - Monitor hematuria; if hematuria persists or recurs, obtain urine dipstick/urinalysis and urine culture.
  - If hematuria is persistent or if stone is suspected clinically (worsening pain, colic, flank pain), consider further evaluation (imaging/urology referral) — to be arranged if indicated on follow-up.

Issue 3: Possible urethritis/STI (alternative diagnosis to consider)
- Assessment:
  - Urethritis from Chlamydia/Gonorrhea is a plausible alternative given sexual history and lack of prior STI screening.
- Plan:
  - Offer STI testing (NAAT for Chlamydia and Gonorrhea) if symptoms persist, if there is clinical suspicion, or per local screening guidance; discuss partner testing/notification if STI confirmed.
  - Consider testing earlier if there is any new discharge, persistent dysuria despite antibiotics, or ongoing risk concerns.

General plan items:
- Pregnancy test recommended to rule out pregnancy if any uncertainty prior to/while treating (clinician advised doing a pregnancy test).
- If no clinical improvement by the end of the week or if systemic features develop, reassess and consider urine microscopy/culture, STI testing, and escalation of care for possible ascending infection (pyelonephritis).
- Documentation to include exact antibiotic choice, dose, route and duration when prescription issued; patient advised to call for clarification if needed.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: no formal vital signs recorded; no physical examination findings documented; no urine dipstick/urinalysis, urine culture, STI NAAT, or pregnancy test performed/documented.
- Medication documentation gap: antibiotic name recommended but specific dose/route/frequency not documented (clinician stated "one tablet twice a day for three days" but did not state exact drug dose or route).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none noted (DDx prioritization is consistent with clinician impression).
- Transcript quality: audio/communication adequate; history obtained thoroughly though no physical exam or investigations were recorded in the transcript.
